blocks.body:
The equation $x^2 - 2y^2 = 1$ has the solutions $(3, 2)$, $(17, 12)$, $(99, 70)$, $(577, 408)$, and they keep coming. The equation $x^2 - 61y^2 = 1$ also has solutions, but the smallest one with $y > 0$ is

$$x = 1766319049, \qquad y = 226153980,$$

and Fermat set exactly this case, together with $d = 109$, as a challenge to other mathematicians in 1657. Brahmagupta had already solved $x^2 - 92y^2 = 1$ in 628 (smallest solution $1151^2 - 92 \cdot 120^2 = 1$) and had discovered how to combine two solutions into a third.

For a positive integer $d$ that is not a perfect square, $x^2 - dy^2 = 1$ is called Pell's equation. This lesson shows that it always has a nontrivial solution, that all solutions are powers of a single fundamental one, and that the [[continued-fractions|continued fraction]] of $\sqrt d$ finds it.

blocks.title: Composing solutions
blocks.body:
Factor the left side over the real numbers: $x^2 - dy^2 = (x + y\sqrt d)(x - y\sqrt d)$. For numbers $\xi = x + y\sqrt d$ with integers $x, y$ define the conjugate $\bar\xi = x - y\sqrt d$ and the norm

$$N(\xi) = \xi \bar\xi = x^2 - dy^2.$$

Because $\sqrt d$ is irrational, the integers $x, y$ are determined by $\xi$. Conjugation respects products, $\overline{\xi\eta} = \bar\xi\, \bar\eta$, as one checks by expanding, so the norm is multiplicative: $N(\xi\eta) = N(\xi) N(\eta)$. Written out, this is Brahmagupta's identity

$$(x_1^2 - d y_1^2)(x_2^2 - d y_2^2) = (x_1 x_2 + d y_1 y_2)^2 - d (x_1 y_2 + x_2 y_1)^2.$$

So if $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$ solve Pell's equation, so does $(x_1x_2 + dy_1y_2,\ x_1y_2 + x_2y_1)$. In particular, from one solution $\varepsilon = x_1 + y_1\sqrt d$ we get infinitely many, the powers $\varepsilon^k$. For $d = 2$ and $\varepsilon = 3 + 2\sqrt 2$:

$$\varepsilon^2 = 17 + 12\sqrt 2, \qquad \varepsilon^3 = 99 + 70\sqrt 2, \qquad \varepsilon^4 = 577 + 408\sqrt 2.$$

Also $\varepsilon^{-1} = \bar\varepsilon = x_1 - y_1\sqrt d$ when $N(\varepsilon) = 1$, so negative powers have integer coordinates too.

blocks.title: Fundamental solution
blocks.body:
The fundamental solution of $x^2 - dy^2 = 1$ is the solution $(x_1, y_1)$ in positive integers with $x_1$ as small as possible. Equivalently, $\varepsilon = x_1 + y_1\sqrt d$ is the smallest number greater than $1$ of the form $x + y\sqrt d$ with $x^2 - dy^2 = 1$.

The two descriptions agree because, among positive solutions, $y = \sqrt{(x^2 - 1)/d}$ increases with $x$, and so does $x + y\sqrt d$; and, as the proof below shows, every such number greater than $1$ has $x > 0$ and $y > 0$.

blocks.title: Structure of the solutions
blocks.body:
Let $d > 0$ be a non-square. Then $x^2 - dy^2 = 1$ has a solution with $y \ne 0$ (Lagrange, 1768). If $(x_1, y_1)$ is the fundamental solution, then the solutions in positive integers are exactly the pairs $(x_k, y_k)$, $k \ge 1$, given by

$$x_k + y_k\sqrt d = (x_1 + y_1 \sqrt d)^k,$$

and all integer solutions are given by $x + y\sqrt d = \pm (x_1 + y_1\sqrt d)^k$ with $k \in \mathbb{Z}$.

blocks.title: Proof that every solution is a power
blocks.body:
We prove existence in the next section; here assume a positive solution exists, so the fundamental one $\varepsilon = x_1 + y_1\sqrt d > 1$ exists too.

Let $(x, y)$ be a positive solution and $u = x + y\sqrt d > 1$. Since $\varepsilon > 1$, the powers $\varepsilon^k$ increase to infinity, so there is $k \ge 0$ with $\varepsilon^k \le u < \varepsilon^{k+1}$. Put $v = u\, \varepsilon^{-k}$. Because $\varepsilon^{-1} = x_1 - y_1\sqrt d$, the number $v$ has the form $a + b\sqrt d$ with integers $a, b$, and by multiplicativity $N(v) = N(u) N(\varepsilon)^{-k} = 1$. Also $1 \le v < \varepsilon$.

Suppose $v > 1$. Its conjugate is $\bar v = 1/v \in (0, 1)$, so

$$a = \frac{v + \bar v}{2} > 0, \qquad b\sqrt d = \frac{v - \bar v}{2} > 0.$$

Then $(a, b)$ is a positive solution with $a + b\sqrt d < \varepsilon$, contradicting the minimality of $\varepsilon$. Hence $v = 1$ and $u = \varepsilon^k$ (with $k \ge 1$, since $u > 1$).

For an arbitrary integer solution $(x, y)$, the number $\xi = x + y\sqrt d$ has $\xi \bar\xi = 1$, and one of the four numbers $\pm\xi, \pm\bar\xi$ equals $|x| + |y|\sqrt d$. That number is $1$ if $y = 0$, and otherwise it is $\varepsilon^k$ with $k \ge 1$ by what we just proved. Undoing the sign and conjugation (recall $\bar\varepsilon = \varepsilon^{-1}$) gives $\xi = \pm \varepsilon^k$ for some $k \in \mathbb Z$.

blocks.title: Why a solution always exists
blocks.body:
The idea is that very good rational approximations $p/q$ to $\sqrt d$ make $p^2 - dq^2$ small, and a pigeonhole argument turns many small values into the value $1$.

Step 1: many small norms. The convergents $p/q$ of $\sqrt d$ satisfy $|\sqrt d - p/q| < 1/q^2$, i.e. $|p - q\sqrt d| < 1/q$. Then $|p + q\sqrt d| < 2q\sqrt d + 1/q$, so

$$|p^2 - dq^2| = |p - q\sqrt d|\,|p + q\sqrt d| < 2\sqrt d + \frac{1}{q^2} \le 2\sqrt d + 1.$$

There are infinitely many convergents and only finitely many integers in this range, and $p^2 - dq^2 \ne 0$ because $\sqrt d$ is irrational. So some nonzero integer $N$ equals $p^2 - dq^2$ for infinitely many convergents.

Step 2: pigeonhole on residues. Among these infinitely many pairs $(p, q)$, there are only $N^2$ possibilities for $(p \bmod |N|,\ q \bmod |N|)$, so we can pick two different convergents $(p_1, q_1) \ne (p_2, q_2)$ with $p_1 \equiv p_2$ and $q_1 \equiv q_2 \pmod{|N|}$.

Step 3: divide. Consider

$$\xi = \frac{(p_1 + q_1 \sqrt d)(p_2 - q_2 \sqrt d)}{N} = \frac{p_1 p_2 - d q_1 q_2}{N} + \frac{q_1 p_2 - p_1 q_2}{N}\sqrt d.$$

Modulo $|N|$ we have $p_1p_2 - dq_1q_2 \equiv p_1^2 - dq_1^2 = N \equiv 0$ and $q_1 p_2 - p_1 q_2 \equiv q_1p_1 - p_1q_1 = 0$, so $\xi = x + y\sqrt d$ with integers $x, y$. Its norm is $N \cdot N / N^2 = 1$. Finally $y \ne 0$, because $q_1p_2 = p_1q_2$ would mean $p_1/q_1 = p_2/q_2$, and distinct convergents are distinct fractions. So $(|x|, |y|)$ is a positive solution.

blocks.title: Finding the fundamental solution
blocks.body:
The existence proof is not a practical algorithm, but continued fractions are. As noted in the lesson on continued fractions, for a positive non-square $d$

$$\sqrt d = [a_0; \overline{a_1, \dots, a_{r-1}, 2a_0}]$$

with period length $r$. Let $p_k/q_k$ be the convergents. The classical result (proved in Chapter 7 of Niven, Zuckerman and Montgomery) is:

1. $p_{r-1}^2 - d\, q_{r-1}^2 = (-1)^r$, and among the numbers $p_k^2 - dq_k^2$ with $k \ge 0$ the values $\pm 1$ occur only at indices $k \equiv -1 \pmod r$.
2. If $r$ is even, the fundamental solution of $x^2 - dy^2 = 1$ is $(p_{r-1}, q_{r-1})$.
3. If $r$ is odd, $(p_{r-1}, q_{r-1})$ solves $x^2 - dy^2 = -1$ instead, and the fundamental solution of $x^2 - dy^2 = 1$ is $(p_{2r-1}, q_{2r-1})$, which is also obtained by squaring: $(p_{r-1} + q_{r-1}\sqrt d)^2$.

In particular the negative Pell equation $x^2 - dy^2 = -1$ is solvable exactly when the period is odd. For $d = 61$ the period is $11$, and this explains the size of the answer: the convergent at index $10$ solves the $-1$ equation, and its square is the solution quoted in the introduction.

blocks.title: The case d = 7
blocks.body: Use the continued fraction $\sqrt 7 = [2; \overline{1, 1, 1, 4}]$ to find the fundamental solution of $x^2 - 7y^2 = 1$, then the next two solutions.
blocks.solution:
The period is $r = 4$, which is even, so the answer is the convergent $p_3/q_3$. From the recurrence $p_k = a_k p_{k-1} + p_{k-2}$, $q_k = a_k q_{k-1} + q_{k-2}$:

$$\frac{p_0}{q_0} = \frac21, \quad \frac{p_1}{q_1} = \frac31, \quad \frac{p_2}{q_2} = \frac52, \quad \frac{p_3}{q_3} = \frac83.$$

Check: $8^2 - 7 \cdot 3^2 = 64 - 63 = 1$. So $\varepsilon = 8 + 3\sqrt 7$. Then

$$\varepsilon^2 = 64 + 63 + 48\sqrt 7 = 127 + 48\sqrt 7, \qquad \varepsilon^3 = (8 + 3\sqrt 7)(127 + 48\sqrt 7) = 2024 + 765\sqrt 7.$$

Check: $127^2 - 7\cdot 48^2 = 16129 - 16128 = 1$ and $2024^2 - 7 \cdot 765^2 = 4096576 - 4096575 = 1$. In general, the $x$-coordinates satisfy $x_{k+1} = 16x_k - x_{k-1}$, since $\varepsilon$ and $\bar\varepsilon$ are roots of $t^2 - 16t + 1$.

blocks.title: An odd period: d = 13
blocks.body: Given $\sqrt{13} = [3; \overline{1, 1, 1, 1, 6}]$, find the smallest positive solutions of $x^2 - 13y^2 = -1$ and of $x^2 - 13y^2 = 1$.
blocks.solution:
The convergents are

$$\frac31,\quad \frac41,\quad \frac72,\quad \frac{11}{3},\quad \frac{18}{5}, \dots$$

The period is $r = 5$, which is odd, so $p_4/q_4 = 18/5$ gives $18^2 - 13 \cdot 5^2 = 324 - 325 = -1$.

Squaring, $(18 + 5\sqrt{13})^2 = 324 + 325 + 180\sqrt{13} = 649 + 180\sqrt{13}$, and indeed $649^2 - 13 \cdot 180^2 = 421201 - 421200 = 1$. So $(649, 180)$ is the fundamental solution of the Pell equation, and $(18, 5)$ the smallest solution of the negative one. Note that the convergents up to $p_4/q_4$ give norms $-4, 3, -3, 4, -1$; none of the small ones is $+1$, which is why trying small $y$ by hand would take $180$ steps.

blocks.title: Square triangular numbers
blocks.body: For which positive integers $n$ is the triangular number $1 + 2 + \dots + n = \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$ a perfect square?
blocks.solution:
We need $n(n+1)/2 = m^2$. Multiply by $8$ and add $1$:

$$4n^2 + 4n + 1 = 8m^2 + 1 \iff (2n+1)^2 - 8m^2 = 1.$$

So $(X, Y) = (2n + 1, m)$ is a positive solution of $X^2 - 8Y^2 = 1$. Conversely every positive solution has $X$ odd (since $X^2 = 8Y^2 + 1$ is odd), so it gives $n = (X-1)/2 \ge 1$ and $m = Y$.

The fundamental solution of $X^2 - 8Y^2 = 1$ is $(3, 1)$, as $Y = 1$ already works. By the structure theorem all positive solutions are $X_k + Y_k\sqrt 8 = (3 + \sqrt 8)^k$, i.e.

$$X_{k+1} = 3X_k + 8Y_k, \qquad Y_{k+1} = X_k + 3Y_k.$$

This gives $(3, 1), (17, 6), (99, 35), (577, 204), (3363, 1189), \dots$, so

$$n = 1,\ 8,\ 49,\ 288,\ 1681,\ \dots, \qquad \frac{n(n+1)}{2} = 1^2,\ 6^2,\ 35^2,\ 204^2,\ 1189^2,\ \dots$$

and these are all of them. For example $\tfrac{49 \cdot 50}{2} = 1225 = 35^2$ and $\tfrac{288 \cdot 289}{2} = 41616 = 204^2$.

blocks.body:
- If $d$ is a perfect square, say $d = c^2$, then $(x - cy)(x + cy) = 1$ forces $y = 0$: only trivial solutions. If $d < 0$ there are finitely many. The theory here needs $d > 0$ non-square.
- The negative equation $x^2 - dy^2 = -1$ is often unsolvable: for $d = 7$, it would need $x^2 \equiv -1 \equiv 6 \pmod 7$, but the squares modulo $7$ are $0, 1, 2, 4$. Do not assume the $\pm$ versions behave alike.
- The fundamental solution can be enormous relative to $d$ ($d = 61$ above). Archimedes' cattle problem leads to $x^2 - 410286423278424\,y^2 = 1$, whose smallest solution has more than a hundred thousand digits. Searching small $y$ is not a method.
- For $x^2 - dy^2 = N$ with $|N| > 1$ the solutions fall into finitely many families, each of the form $\xi\, \varepsilon^k$, but there can be several families or none. Multiplying by powers of $\varepsilon$ does not generate them from a single one in general.

The numbers $x + y\sqrt d$ with $x^2 - dy^2 = \pm 1$ are exactly the units (invertible elements) of the ring $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d]$, and the structure theorem says the units of norm $1$ form the group $\{\pm \varepsilon^k\}$. The fundamental solution is the fundamental unit of $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d]$ (its smallest unit greater than $1$), or the square of that unit when it has norm $-1$, as for $d = 13$, where $18 + 5\sqrt{13}$ has norm $-1$. This is the simplest case of Dirichlet's unit theorem in the theory of [[ideals|rings of integers]]. A related number, the regulator, appears in the [[class-number-formula]] for the real quadratic field $\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)$. It is the logarithm of the fundamental unit of the full ring of integers, which can be a root of $\varepsilon$: for $d = 13$ that unit is $\tfrac{3 + \sqrt{13}}{2}$, whose sixth power is $649 + 180\sqrt{13}$.

Pell equations arise whenever a [[diophantine]] problem reduces to a quadratic in two variables: square triangular numbers, Pythagorean triangles with legs differing by $1$, and many olympiad problems. They also appear in [[vieta-jumping]], where the descent moves along the same hyperbolas, and in the study of indefinite [[quadratic-forms|binary quadratic forms]], whose automorphisms are built from Pell solutions. The fact that solutions grow like $\varepsilon^k$ ties back to [[diophantine-approx|Diophantine approximation]]: $x/y$ approximates $\sqrt d$ with error about $1/(2\sqrt d\, y^2)$.

1. Find the fundamental solutions of $x^2 - dy^2 = 1$ for $d = 3, 5, 6, 10$.
2. Prove that $x^2 - 3y^2 = -1$ has no integer solutions, and determine whether $x^2 - 5y^2 = -1$ does.
3. Show that there are infinitely many Pythagorean triples whose legs are consecutive integers, and find the first three.
4. If $(x_1, y_1)$ is the fundamental solution, show that $x_{k+1} = 2x_1 x_k - x_{k-1}$ for $k \ge 1$, with $x_0 = 1$.
